kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை போற்றுவார்
போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral ikazhaamai potruvaar
potraluL ellaam thalai.
kurals.meaning: Of all the precautions a careful person can take to protect themselves, the first and best is never to belittle the strength of those who are able to accomplish what they set out to do.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a small puppy barking and nipping at a big, calm elephant. The safest thing the puppy can do is simply not tease the elephant. Being respectful to people who are strong and capable is the best way to keep yourself out of trouble.
kurals.university: The opening couplet frames the whole adhikaram as a matter of self-protection: poatruvaar (போற்றுவார், those who guard themselves) have many kinds of poatral (போற்றல், guarding, watchfulness), but the thalai (தலை, head, foremost) of them all is ikazhaamai (இகழாமை, not despising) the aatral (ஆற்றல், power, capability) of aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், those able to carry out what they undertake). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar, reads the chapter in the setting of statecraft: having discussed internal enmity (Ch. 89), Valluvar now warns the king and his men against offending two classes of the great, the mighty in worldly power and the great in spiritual power (ascetics). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss aatruvaar as one able to complete a chosen task, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as those who lead and guide. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, when Krishna comes to the Kaurava court as an envoy of peace, Duryodhana and his allies scheme to seize him, underestimating him; Krishna reveals his overwhelming divine form and the plot collapses.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana treated a being of immense power as an ordinary messenger who could be bound, and the episode foreshadows the ruin that followed his contempt.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s first safeguard is exactly what Duryodhana neglected: never despise the power of those able to act.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana sub-parva), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A well-known narrative of slighting the mighty; it illustrates the principle rather than stating it as a maxim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; And to esteem them very highly in love for their work’s sake.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks the Thessalonian church to recognize and highly esteem those who labour and lead among them, precisely because of the work they do.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties respect to the capacity and accomplishment of those who do the work, though without the Kural’s warning of danger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of esteeming capable workers, but the Kural’s motive is prudent self-protection rather than love.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The verse commands believers to give due obedience and regard to the Prophet and to those holding rightful authority.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly counsels not to slight those who hold real power, though it frames this as wise caution rather than obedience.
islam._accuracy_note: Related idea of regard for authority; the Kural’s specific point, not underrating others’ power, is only implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, and the honor of your colleague as the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher as the reverence of heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua sets up a ladder of honor in which reverence for one’s teacher approaches reverence for God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s chapter likewise places due regard for the great among the highest of duties.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on honoring the great; it lacks the Kural’s emphasis on their power to harm.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To one ever eager to revere and serve the elders, these four blessing accrue: long life and beauty, happiness and power.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that steady reverence for elders brings concrete benefits to the one who shows it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present respect for the great as something that protects and benefits the respectful person.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Positive framing of the same principle; the Kural speaks of the danger avoided, the Dhammapada of blessings gained.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne boasts that her weaving surpasses that of Athena, refuses the goddess’s warning, and after the contest is transformed into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mortal who scorned the skill and power of a goddess lost her own human form as a result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Arachne did exactly what the Kural warns against: she made light of the power of one far more capable.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel to slighting a superior power; the divine setting differs from the Kural’s political one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now slighting is the actively entertained opinion of something as obviously of no importance. … clearly you do not think that he can do you harm, for then you would be afraid of him instead of slighting him …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines anger as a painful impulse to revenge for an unjustified slight, and observes that we slight only those we judge unable to harm us; if we thought them capable, we would fear them instead.
philosophy.tie_back: To belittle someone is to misjudge his power, and the Kural's first safeguard is never to make that error about people who are able to act.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, II.2, 1378b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Rhys Roberts); spacing artefacts in the online text normalised. Next-best partial match: Aristotle analyses slighting and the anger it provokes, and he does not himself give the Kural's prudential warning against belittling capable people.

kurals.tamil:
பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகிற் பெரியாரால்
பேரா இடும்பை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Periyaaraip penaadhu ozhukir periyaaraal
peraa itumpai tharum.
kurals.meaning: If a person conducts himself without showing due regard to the great, that very disregard will bring him lasting, irremovable trouble at their hands.
kurals.elementary: If you keep ignoring your coach and being rude, you might find yourself benched for the whole season. Not treating important people with respect can bring trouble that doesn’t go away quickly.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the repeated periyaar (பெரியார், the great): conduct (ozhugal, ஒழுகல்) that does not penu (பேணு, cherish, honour) the great yields, through those same great ones, peraa idumbai (பேரா இடும்பை, affliction that does not depart). The adjective peraa (from pe-, to move away) stresses permanence, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as நீங்காத துன்பம். Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it simply as disrespect to elders or great persons, while the traditional reading behind Pope’s explanation glosses periyaar as powerful rulers. The phrase periyaaraal (by the great) shows that the harm is not mere fate but the active response of the offended party. Both sources agree on the text, including the sandhi form ஒழுகிற்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Abhijnanashakuntalam, Shakuntala, lost in thoughts of Dushyanta, fails to greet the visiting sage Durvasa, who curses her that her beloved will forget her; much of the play’s suffering follows.
hinduism.explanation: A single lapse in honouring a great ascetic brings a long chain of sorrow that is only lifted much later.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s peraa idumbai: lasting trouble that comes from the very great one who was neglected.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close narrative match: neglect of a great one leads to prolonged suffering, though Shakuntala’s lapse was innocent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that opposing rightful authority brings judgment upon the one who resists.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that defying those in power returns as heavy consequence on oneself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared idea of consequences for defying authority; Paul grounds it in divine order, the Kural in practical prudence.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet or be loud to him in speech like the loudness of some of you to others, lest your deeds become worthless while you perceive not.”
islam.explanation: Believers are warned that even careless disrespect toward the Prophet can quietly nullify their good deeds.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, failing to honour the great carries a serious and lasting loss, sometimes unnoticed until too late.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct teaching about irreverence toward a great person and its lasting cost.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet advises against even private contempt for the powerful, since word of it will reach them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that disregard for the great returns as trouble from the great themselves.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close practical parallel about the danger of disrespecting the powerful.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with the foolish, but to associate with the wise; and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists honouring those worthy of honour among the highest blessings of life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the reverse side: failing to honour the great invites lasting harm.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same value expressed positively; no mention of the consequences that the Kural stresses.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Agamemnon rudely dismisses Chryses, priest of Apollo, who comes to ransom his daughter; Apollo answers the priest’s prayer with a plague on the Greek camp.
greek_mythology.explanation: Insulting a man under divine protection brought sustained disaster on the whole army until the wrong was put right.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s contempt for a great one’s claim produced the Kural’s trouble that comes through the great.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel: disrespect to a priest leads to prolonged suffering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates tells the Athenian jurors that if they put him to death they will harm themselves more than him, and will not easily find another like him.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a city which mistreats its wisest citizen injures itself most of all.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly holds that disregarding the great rebounds as lasting harm on the offender.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel; Socrates speaks of moral and civic self-harm rather than the great one’s retaliation.

kurals.tamil:
கெடல்வேண்டின் கேளாது செய்க அடல்வேண்டின்
ஆற்று பவர்கண் இழுக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ketalventin kelaadhu seyka atalventin
aatru pavarkan izhukku.
kurals.meaning: If a person wants to bring ruin on himself, let him, without heeding anyone, commit offences against those who are able to destroy whenever they wish.
kurals.elementary: If you poke a sleeping bear with a stick and ignore everyone shouting stop, you are asking for trouble. Valluvar says, with a wink: if you want to get hurt, go ahead and annoy the strongest one around.
kurals.university: This couplet uses irony: keDal veNDin (கெடல் வேண்டின், if you desire ruin), keLaadhu seyga (கேளாது செய்க, do it without listening), izhukku (இழுக்கு, offence, fault) toward aatrupavar (ஆற்றுபவர், those able) aDal veNDin (அடல் வேண்டின், when they wish to slay). The phrase keLaadhu is read differently: Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, takes it as not listening to the righteous dictates of law or the nīti texts, and Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ignoring what the moral treatises say; Kalaignar reads it as not listening to anyone’s advice; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first half more freely as a separate clause. The pairing keDal/aDal is a typical Valluvar sound-echo. The text is identical in both sources, which print ஆற்று பவர்கண் with the metrical split.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yuddha Kanda, Ravana rejects the repeated counsel of his brother Vibhishana to return Sita to Rama, insults him, and drives him away, then goes on to his destruction.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana refused to listen to wise advice and persisted in offending a far mightier opponent until his kingdom fell.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s formula for ruin exactly: do not listen, and wrong the one who can destroy you.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match combining both elements of the couplet, ignoring counsel and offending the mighty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that one who keeps refusing correction will meet sudden and irreparable ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s keLaadhu, refusing to listen, is the same road to ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the refusal-to-listen element; the offence against the mighty is not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, ‘If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.’”
islam.explanation: The people of the Fire lament too late that they refused to listen and reason when warned.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it traces ruin to the refusal to heed.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on not listening leading to ruin; eschatological rather than political setting.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the elders who served his father Solomon, follows the harsh advice of his young companions, and ten tribes break away from his kingdom.
judaism.explanation: By refusing to heed experienced counsellors and provoking the people, Rehoboam lost most of his realm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s path to self-ruin, acting without listening, is exactly Rehoboam’s choice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on refusing counsel; the offended party is the people rather than a single mighty figure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever, on account of perverted views, scorns the Teaching of the Perfected Ones, the Noble and Righteous Ones — that fool, like the bamboo, produces fruits only for self destruction.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares one who scorns the noble ones to a bamboo whose own fruiting kills it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, scorning the great is described as a self-chosen path to ruin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: contempt for the great as self-destruction.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Bacchae, King Pentheus ignores the warnings of the seer Tiresias and of his grandfather Cadmus, persecutes the god Dionysus, and is destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pentheus refused all counsel and made war on a power far greater than his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He follows the Kural’s ironic recipe for ruin to the letter.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on both refusal of counsel and offence against a mightier being.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Plato describes a ship whose quarrelling sailors ignore and mock the true navigator, so that the voyage is ruined.
philosophy.explanation: A community that will not listen to those with real skill steers itself toward disaster.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly links ruin to refusing to heed and disrespecting the capable.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Looser parallel about ignoring expertise; it lacks the retaliation of a mighty person.

kurals.tamil:
கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால் ஆற்றுவார்க்கு
ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kootraththaik kaiyaal viliththatraal aatruvaarkku
aatraadhaar innaa seyal.
kurals.meaning: When the powerless do harm to the powerful, it is like beckoning Death with one’s own hand to come and take them.
kurals.elementary: A tiny mouse that pulls a lion’s tail is basically waving and calling, Come and get me! When someone weak picks a fight with someone much stronger, they are inviting their own trouble.
kurals.university: The image is vivid: kootram (கூற்றம், Death, Yama, the god who divides life from body) is summoned kaiyaal viLiththu (கையால் விளித்து, by beckoning with the hand). The comparison applies to aatraadhaar (ஆற்றாதார், those without power) doing innaa (இன்னா, harm) to aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், the powerful). Solomon Pappaiah specifies the three kinds of power, of wisdom, wealth and army, and adds that it is the weak who strike first; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses that Yama would come of himself anyway, so the weak only hasten it. The couplet carries forward kural 891’s key word aatruvaar, binding the chapter together. Text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Shishupala heaps insults on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice; after his hundredth offence Krishna’s discus slays him.
hinduism.explanation: A ruler who kept provoking a far greater power, despite warnings, called his own death upon himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Shishupala is the Kural’s weak man beckoning Death with his own hand.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Sisupala-badha), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative illustration of the weak provoking the mighty unto death.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to the common sense of a king who weighs his strength before going to war against a stronger foe.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural warns of what happens when the weaker side skips that reckoning and strikes anyway.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the weak-versus-strong calculation; Jesus uses it as a parable about discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: Surah al-Fil recalls how the army of the elephant marched to destroy the Kaaba and was struck down, made like eaten straw.
islam.explanation: A force that attacked what God protected was destroyed despite its apparent might.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, assaulting a far greater power brings one’s own destruction.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the attackers were mighty in worldly terms, but powerless before God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says that provoking a ruler’s anger is like sending for death, and the wise avoid it.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own image of summoning Death by provoking the powerful.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image: angering the powerful as calling messengers of death.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Nidanakatha tells how Mara and his army assailed the Bodhisatta beneath the Bodhi tree with storms and weapons, and were utterly routed.
buddhism.explanation: Even a host of attackers could not prevail against one of supreme spiritual strength.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the futility of the weaker attacking the truly mighty that the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Birth Stories)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Thematic only; Mara is defeated rather than killed, and the episode is about awakening, not prudence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas challenges Apollo to a musical contest, loses, and is flayed alive as punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: A lesser being who challenged a god paid for it with his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Marsyas beckoned his own doom by provoking a far stronger power, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear narrative parallel of the weak challenging the mighty unto death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence, though an obstinate fight may be made by a small force, in the end it must be captured by the larger force.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu observes that a weaker force that insists on fighting a stronger one will in the end be overwhelmed.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the strategic version of the Kural’s warning that the weak who strike the strong invite their own end.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.10 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in substance; Sun Tzu speaks of armies, the Kural of any weak person harming the strong.

kurals.tamil:
யாண்டுச்சென்று யாண்டும் உளராகார் வெந்துப்பின்
வேந்து செறப்பட் டவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaantuchchendru yaantum ularaakaar vendhuppin
vendhu serappat tavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who have earned the anger of a king of fierce strength will not survive anywhere, wherever they may flee.
kurals.elementary: Playing hide-and-seek with someone who can see everywhere is no fun, because there is nowhere to hide. If you make a very powerful ruler angry, no hiding place is safe.
kurals.university: Here the great one is a vendhu (வேந்து, king) of vem-thuppu (வெந்துப்பு, fierce strength); those seRappaTTavar (செறப்பட்டவர், who have incurred his wrath, from seRu, to be angry) will be uLar aakaar (உளர் ஆகார், will not exist, will not live) yaaNDu senRu yaaNDum (wherever they go, anywhere). Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Varadarasanar agree that the offender cannot live anywhere; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads uLar aakaar more psychologically, as being unable to settle. Pope’s rendering notes they will not prosper wherever they go. The two sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net’s transliteration shows the metrical division வெந்துப்பின் / வேந்து, with the split செறப்பட் டவர் in both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sita recalls how a crow (Kakasura) that wounded her was pursued by a grass blade Rama charged as a missile; the crow fled through the worlds, but no god would shelter it, until it returned to Rama himself for refuge.
hinduism.explanation: No place in any world offered protection from the wrath of the one it had offended.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: wherever the offender flees, there is no refuge from a mighty ruler’s anger.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (the crow episode recounted by Sita)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative parallel; the story ends in mercy, which the Kural does not envisage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb.”
christianity.explanation: John’s vision shows all ranks of people trying in vain to hide from divine wrath.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, there is no hiding place from the anger of the supreme ruler.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong image of futile flight from a throne’s wrath; divine rather than human king.

islam.quote_or_event: “Man will say on that Day, ‘Where is the [place of] escape?’ No! There is no refuge.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment people search for an escape and find none.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who angers the mighty finds no place to survive.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the no-escape idea; eschatological rather than political.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonah tries to flee from God’s command by sailing to Tarshish, but a storm and a great fish bring him back.
judaism.explanation: The prophet learns that there is no running away from the Sovereign he tried to evade.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s offender, Jonah found that flight to distant places does not escape a mighty ruler.
judaism._accuracy_note: Fits the futility of flight; Jonah disobeyed rather than offended, and is spared.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no place in the world shelters one from the fruit of one’s evil acts.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same no-escape logic to the wrath of a mighty king.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in structure; the pursuer is karma rather than a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother, Orestes is hounded from land to land by the Furies and finds no rest until he reaches Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: The avenging powers pursue him wherever he goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s image of one who can find no place to live after angering a great power.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares the futile-flight motif; Orestes’ guilt and eventual acquittal differ from the Kural’s case.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius, once a high official, fell foul of King Theodoric, was imprisoned and condemned, and wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution.
philosophy.explanation: Even a man of great standing could not escape once he had lost the favour of a powerful king.
philosophy.tie_back: His fate illustrates the Kural’s warning about incurring a mighty ruler’s anger, though Boethius protested his innocence.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I (author’s circumstances)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Historical illustration only; the Consolation itself teaches detachment, not caution toward kings.

kurals.tamil:
எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார்
பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Eriyaal sutappatinum uyvuntaam uyyaar
periyaarp pizhaiththozhuku vaar.
kurals.meaning: Someone caught and burnt by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not escape.
kurals.elementary: Getting burnt by a campfire hurts, but you can heal. Valluvar says that hurting truly great people is even more dangerous than fire, because there may be no getting better from it.
kurals.university: The comparison is a fortiori: eri (எரி, fire) can burn a man and still uyvu uNDaam (உய்வு உண்டாம், there may be escape, survival), but uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) who periyaarp pizhaiththu ozhuguvaar (பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், live in offence against the great). The chapter title itself comes from this root, pizhai (பிழை, fault, offence). Pope’s explanation, reflecting the traditional commentary, glosses the fire as a forest fire and the great as devotees or ascetics, whose spiritual power is pictured as more consuming than physical flame. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the great as those of surpassing power generally. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sixty thousand sons of King Sagara, searching for the sacrificial horse, accuse and assault the sage Kapila in his hermitage, and are reduced to ashes by his power.
hinduism.explanation: Their offence against a great sage destroyed them instantly and completely.
hinduism.tie_back: Here the sage’s power literally acts as fire, matching the Kural’s claim that offending the great is deadlier than fire.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (sargas 39-40, the sons of Sagara)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel, including the fire image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
christianity.explanation: The writer warns that those who scorn what is holy face a judgment more terrible than any human punishment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural also ranks offending the great as worse than being burnt by fire.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the sense of a fate worse than physical harm; the object is God, not great persons.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abraham’s people cast him into a fire for opposing their idols, God commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for him, and he came out unharmed.
islam.explanation: Abraham survived literal fire because he stood with God, while those who opposed him failed.
islam.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s point that fire can be survived, while the real danger lies in opposing the truly great.
islam._accuracy_note: Weak, indirect match built on the survivable-fire image; paraphrased.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Warm yourself before the fire of the wise, but beware of being singed by their glowing coals, for their bite is the bite of a fox, and their sting is the sting of a scorpion, and their hiss is the hiss of a serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the sages give warmth to those who approach rightly but burn those who offend them.
judaism.tie_back: This is a remarkably close parallel: the great are like fire, and offending them burns worse than flame.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: the sages’ power pictured as fire that burns those who wrong them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm aimed at a pure person blows back on the one who throws it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, offending the virtuous great is a fault from which the offender does not escape.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in principle; the mechanism is karmic recoil rather than the great one’s anger.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ajax the Lesser, hated by Athena, escapes shipwreck with Poseidon’s help, but when he boasts that he has escaped despite the gods, Poseidon splits the rock and he drowns.
greek_mythology.explanation: He survived the physical danger of the sea but not his defiance of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s man who survives fire, Ajax survived the storm but could not survive offending the great.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good structural parallel of surviving the elements yet perishing for defiance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates recalls that the poet Stesichorus was struck blind for speaking ill of Helen and regained his sight only after composing a recantation.
philosophy.explanation: Even a famous poet suffered for defaming a revered figure, and was restored only by making amends.
philosophy.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s warning that offending the great brings a penalty one cannot simply walk away from.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Thematic only; Stesichorus recovers, whereas the Kural denies escape.

kurals.tamil:
வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும் என்னாம்
தகைமாண்ட தக்கார் செறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vakaimaanta vaazhkkaiyum vaanporulum ennaam
thakaimaanta thakkaar serin.
kurals.meaning: If the truly worthy, eminent in character, turn their anger on someone, what use is that person’s splendid life and vast wealth?
kurals.elementary: You could have the biggest toy collection in the world, but if you are mean to the kindest, wisest grown-up in town, everyone will stop trusting you. All your toys can’t fix that. Good people’s goodwill is worth more than riches.
kurals.university: Two pairs balance each other: vagai maaNDa vaazhkkai (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கை, a life excellent in every kind) and vaan poruL (வான்பொருள், sky-high wealth) are worth ennaam (என்னாம், what will they become?) if thagai maaNDa thakkaar (தகைமாண்ட தக்கார், the worthy, distinguished in noble quality) seRin (செறின், are angered). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, applies this to a king whose government with all its auxiliaries and untold wealth is useless before the wrath of the righteous great; Solomon Pappaiah glosses the great as those excellent in character. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the couplet differently, as saying that wealth and splendour cannot equal the richness of the worthy, showing an alternative interpretation of seRin. Both sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Indra carelessly lets his elephant trample a garland given by the sage Durvasa, the sage curses him, and Indra and the gods lose their prosperity and fortune until the churning of the ocean restores it.
hinduism.explanation: All the wealth and splendour of the king of the gods vanished when he slighted a great sage.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim exactly: splendid life and vast wealth are worthless once the worthy great are angered.
hinduism.source: Vishnu Purana, Book 1, Chapter 9 (trans. H. H. Wilson)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match, and a story well known in Tamil tradition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that worldly gain is worthless if the deepest good is lost.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s question, what use are life and wealth, has the same rhetorical shape.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the futility-of-wealth question; the cause of loss differs.

islam.quote_or_event: “His wealth will not avail him or that which he gained.”
islam.explanation: Said of Abu Lahab, who opposed and insulted the Prophet: his riches could not protect him.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares wealth useless to one who sets himself against the great.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: opposition to a great figure renders wealth useless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb teaches that wealth gives no protection when wrath arrives.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says riches count for nothing once the worthy are angered.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on wealth’s uselessness before wrath; the wrath here is divine.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states: Sharp pain, or disaster, bodily injury, serious illness, or derangement of mind, trouble from the government, or grave charges, loss of relatives, or loss of wealth, or houses destroyed by ravaging fire.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the calamities, including loss of wealth and property, that befall one who offends the harmless.
buddhism.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s point that wealth and a fine life collapse when one wrongs the virtuous.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on loss of wealth after offending the virtuous; the verse goes on to rebirth in hell, omitted here.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, a wealthy man, cuts down Demeter’s sacred oak despite warnings, and is cursed with insatiable hunger that devours all his riches.
greek_mythology.explanation: His great wealth was consumed entirely after he offended a goddess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, prosperity proves worthless once the great are angered.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel on lost wealth after offending a great power.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates urges the Athenians to care for virtue above wealth, saying that wealth does not bring excellence, but excellence makes wealth and everything else good.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, riches have no value apart from goodness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly subordinates wealth to the regard of the virtuous.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak match: shares the low view of wealth, not the theme of offending the great.

kurals.tamil:
குன்றன்னார் குன்ற மதிப்பின் குடியொடு
நின்றன்னார் மாய்வர் நிலத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kundrannaar kundra madhippin kutiyotu
nindrannaar maaivar nilaththu.
kurals.meaning: If those who are great like mountains are held in low esteem, or resolve on someone’s ruin, even people who seemed permanently established will perish from the earth together with their families.
kurals.elementary: Think of a mountain: it is big, steady and old. If you try to knock a mountain down, you will only hurt yourself. People who are great like mountains deserve respect, and those who treat them badly can lose everything, even their family’s good name.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on kunRu (குன்று, hill, mountain) and kunRa (குன்ற, to diminish): if kunRannaar (குன்றன்னார், those like mountains) are kunRa madhikkap paDin (thought of as diminished, slighted), or, in another reading, if they madhi (மதி, resolve) on diminishing someone, then even ninRannaar (நின்றன்னார், those who seem to stand forever) maaivar (மாய்வர், will perish) kuDiyoDu (குடியொடு, along with their lineage) nilaththu (நிலத்து, on earth). The two readings are visible in the commentaries: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the mountain-like great resolving on destruction, while Sivayogi Sivakumar and Kalaignar take it as others belittling the great. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, identifies the mountain-like ones as devotees. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Young Yadavas mock the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada by dressing Samba as a pregnant woman; the sages curse that an iron bolt will destroy the race, and the Yadava clan later perishes in fratricidal slaughter.
hinduism.explanation: A jest against great sages led to the destruction of an entire, seemingly invincible dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image of seemingly permanent people perishing with their whole kin for slighting the mountain-like great.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 1, trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: slighting sages destroys a whole established clan.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the rejected cornerstone that breaks those who stumble on it and crushes those it falls upon.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s mountain-like great similarly crush those who set themselves against them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Rock imagery and the crushing of opponents match; the family dimension is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was for him no company to aid him other than Allah, nor was he of those who [could] defend themselves.”
islam.explanation: Qarun, arrogant in his wealth and defiant toward Moses, was swallowed by the earth along with his house.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, one who seemed firmly established perished from the earth together with his household.
islam._accuracy_note: Close parallel including household and the earth; the offence is against God and Moses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their houses, and all the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods.”
judaism.explanation: Korah and his followers, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron, were swallowed by the earth with their households and possessions.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s warning that those who belittle the great perish from the earth with their whole family.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near direct match: opposing the great leads to destruction with one’s household, on the earth itself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Upali Sutta, the Buddha asks whether Upali has heard how the Dandaka, Kalinga, Mejjha and Matanga forests came to be wilderness, and Upali answers that it was through the mental anger of seers.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta recalls a tradition that whole inhabited realms were laid waste because seers were offended.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s picture of established peoples wiped from the earth by the wrath of the great.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the Buddha cites it to argue that mental action is weighty, not to counsel respect.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Niobe boasts that her many children make her greater than the goddess Leto; Apollo and Artemis slay her children, and she is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her pride against a divine mother destroyed her entire family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, belittling the great brings ruin upon oneself together with one’s kin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on ruin with one’s family; tasteful retelling of a tragic myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue, the Melians refuse to yield to the far stronger Athenians, and the city is captured, its men killed and its women and children enslaved.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides shows a small city destroyed as a community after defying a superior power.
philosophy.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that whole households perish when the mighty are slighted, though Thucydides invites sympathy for Melos.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116
philosophy._accuracy_note: Historical parallel only; the moral of the dialogue is ambiguous and critical of the strong.

kurals.tamil:
ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் இடைமுரிந்து
வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Endhiya kolkaiyaar seerin itaimurindhu
vendhanum vendhu ketum.
kurals.meaning: When those who uphold lofty principles rise in anger, even a king will be broken midway and lose his kingdom.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a team captain who bullies the fairest, most honest player. When the whole team sees it and stands with that honest player, the captain loses the job. Even powerful people can fall if they anger those who live by high principles.
kurals.university: Eendhiya koLgaiyaar (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்) are those who bear aloft high principles or vows; if they seeRin (சீறின், flare up in anger), even the vendhan (வேந்தன், king) will iDai murindhu (இடை முரிந்து, be broken midway) and vendhu keDum (வேந்து கெடும், his kingship will perish). Pope’s explanation glosses the king as Indra and the great as those of exalted vows, reflecting the traditional commentary’s allusion to Nahusha, who was cast down from Indra’s throne by the curse of the sage Agastya. Modern commentators generalize: Solomon Pappaiah speaks of a ruler losing office midway, and Kalaignar reads it politically as tyranny collapsing when principled people rise up. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nahusha, raised to the throne of Indra, grows arrogant, makes the great sages carry his palanquin, and kicks Agastya; the sage’s curse hurls him from heaven to earth as a serpent.
hinduism.explanation: A king at the summit of power fell in the middle of his reign because he offended a sage of great vows.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the story traditionally linked to this very couplet: even the king of the gods is broken midway when the great flare up.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sections XI-XVII (Nahusha), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the traditional reading of the kural alludes to this episode.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.”
christianity.explanation: Mary’s song praises God who topples the powerful from their thrones.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says even kings can be brought down from their seats.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the overthrow of rulers; the agent is God, not principled people.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will.’”
islam.explanation: The verse affirms that kingship is given and withdrawn by God.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, no king’s rule is so secure that it cannot be taken away.
islam._accuracy_note: Related on the fragility of kingship; says nothing of offending the righteous.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Uzziah, grown proud, enters the Temple to burn incense, defying the priests who withstand him; he is struck with leprosy while still raging, and lives apart while his son governs.
judaism.explanation: A powerful and successful king was cut off from rule after defying those consecrated to holy service.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s king who is broken midway when he opposes those of high vows.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close narrative parallel; the punishment comes from God rather than from the priests’ anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sarabhanga Jataka, King Dandaki insults the ascetic Kisavaccha, and his kingdom is destroyed, becoming the wilderness later known as the Dandaka forest.
buddhism.explanation: A ruling king lost his realm because he offended an ascetic.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s warning that a king falls when those of lofty vows are provoked.
buddhism.source: Jataka 522, Sarabhanga Jataka (trans. ed. E. B. Cowell)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; details are summarized from secondary knowledge and not checked against the full text.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Diomedes recalls how Lycurgus, king of the Edonians, attacked the nurses of the young Dionysus; Zeus blinded him and he did not live long, hated by all the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king who assaulted the sacred was cut down in the midst of his life and rule.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, even a king is broken midway when he provokes those under divine protection.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; the offended party is a god rather than principled humans.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes in Politics V that many monarchies have been overthrown because of insult and contempt shown toward subjects, which provoke attacks on the ruler.
philosophy.explanation: Rulers who treat people with outrage invite their own overthrow.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that even kings fall when the high-minded are provoked to anger.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Reasonable parallel; Aristotle’s analysis is about revenge for insult generally, not specifically the virtuous.

kurals.tamil:
இறந்தமைந்த சார்புடையர் ஆயினும் உய்யார்
சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Irandhamaindha saarputaiyar aayinum uyyaar
sirandhamaindha seeraar serin.
kurals.meaning: Even those who have boundless support and powerful allies cannot escape if people of outstanding greatness are angered against them.
kurals.elementary: Having lots of friends to stick up for you is great, but if you do something really wrong to a truly good and respected person, even all those friends can’t save you. Being respectful is better protection than having a big gang.
kurals.university: The final couplet sets iRandhu amaindha saarbu (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு, supports exceeding all measure, from iRa, to go beyond) against siRandhu amaindha seeraar (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார், those whose glory is excellently formed). The verb uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) echoes kural 896, and seRin (செறின், if angered) echoes 895 and 897, rounding off the chapter. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, glosses the great here as the noble whose penance is boundless, so the chapter ends where it began, with the two kinds of greatness, worldly and spiritual. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iRandhamaindha as like the dead, that is renunciants, a markedly different interpretation of the first phrase. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Vishvamitra, with his whole army, tries to seize the wish-granting cow of the sage Vasishtha; Vasishtha’s spiritual power destroys his forces and sons, and the king concludes that a warrior’s might is nothing beside a sage’s power.
hinduism.explanation: All the king’s armies and resources could not prevail against the anger of a great sage.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s conclusion: boundless support does not save one who angers the truly great.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (sargas 52-56, Vishvamitra and Vasishtha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match on armies failing against a sage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist declares that neither great armies nor personal strength can secure deliverance.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own claim that vast support cannot save the offender.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close verbal and thematic match on the uselessness of great support.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Day when there will not benefit [anyone] wealth or children”
islam.explanation: Abraham’s prayer describes the Day when the usual supports of wealth and family avail nothing.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, one’s supports, however great, cannot save one in the decisive hour.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the futility of supports; the setting is judgment, not offending the great.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah warns against trusting wisdom, might or riches as one’s security.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly teaches that worldly supports offer no safety against the anger of the great.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the distrust of worldly supports; no reference to offending great persons.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada Commentary, Devadatta, despite the backing of the powerful prince Ajatasattu, plotted repeatedly against the Buddha and was finally swallowed by the earth.
buddhism.explanation: Royal patronage could not save one who set himself against the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, mighty allies do not protect one who offends the truly great.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary, story for verse 17 (trans. E. W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit; the earth-swallowing is a commentarial tradition, not in the canonical Vinaya account.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, boasts that not even Zeus can stop him scaling the walls, and is struck down by Zeus’s thunderbolt despite the great army around him.
greek_mythology.explanation: His boast against a supreme power destroyed him in the midst of a mighty host.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s point that great allies do not save one who provokes the great.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit; the thunderbolt itself is told in later sources, Aeschylus presenting the boast and doom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In a note on Sun Tzu, the commentator Li Ch’uan recalls Fu Chien, who was warned not to despise his enemy but boasted of a million troops, and was soon disastrously routed at the Fei River.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler confident in vast forces fell after scorning a capable opponent.
philosophy.tie_back: This joins the Kural’s last couplet to its first: despising the able cannot be redeemed by numbers.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.18, with Li Ch’uan’s commentary (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Historical anecdote from a commentary; fits the theme though the enemy were generals rather than sages.
